items.alt: Welcome arch at the entrance to Hungduan

children.text: Hungduan, about an hour by jeepney from Banaue, is a valley where World Heritage rice terraces spread like a spider's web across three villages. You can walk the wide Hapao paddies, the sturdy stone walls of Baang and the tall terraces of Nungulunan, and even take in a riverside hot spring and a harvest ritual.
Hungduan is a small municipality in the mountains of southwestern Ifugao, about
24km
by road from central Banaue. About 9,000 people live scattered across rugged terrain that runs from a valley floor at around
up to peaks of more than

, and most of them grow rice and vegetables for a living. The Hungduan rice terraces are one of the five sites of the UNESCO World Heritage property "Rice Terraces of the Philippine Cordilleras," inscribed in

The Hungduan terraces are not one big surface but are divided among three villages. Nungulunan is known for tall, steep paddies, Hapao for wide, gently sloping ones, and Baang for its stone-walled fields. Because the paddies spread out in every direction across the three villages, they are also nicknamed the "spider web terraces." Hapao in particular has gentle slopes and broad paddies, which makes walking the paddy walls relatively easy.

What makes Hungduan even more special is that the terraces and their rituals are still alive together. After the harvest, villagers take part in Punnuk, a tug-of-war in the Hapao River in which two sides pull a ring woven from rice straw. It was inscribed on the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in
, and every year around
August
the people of Hapao, Baang and Nungulunan hold the ritual together. Here the terraces are not just scenery but the calendar and the stage of the community.

While visitors crowd into Banaue and Batad, Hungduan is still quiet. Many days there are only a few photographers and villagers going about the paddy walls, so it suits slow walking trips and travelers who find Banaue too busy or simply want to see World Heritage terraces in peace. Public transport is scarce and lodging is simple, so leave some slack in your schedule.

blocks.title: See the valley from the Hapao viewpoint

children.text: A roadside viewpoint in Hapao has a UNESCO signboard, and below it the wide paddies and village roofs spread out in one view. When the fields are flooded they reflect the sky like mirrors, and once the seedlings are planted the whole valley turns a single shade of green.

blocks.title: Walk the paddy walls from Nungulunan to Hapao to Baang

children.text: This route links the three villages in turn, and following narrow paths along the paddy walls plus stone steps takes about
3 hours
. The shape of the paddies changes from village to village, so the scenery keeps shifting as you walk. The paths branch in many places, so it is safer to go with a licensed guide.
A walk of about
2.5km
through the Hapao paddies brings you to Bogyah Hot Spring by the river. The walk takes around
40 minutes to 1 hour
, and the spring is reported to be open to visitors from about
9 a.m. to 4 p.m.
, after which it is reserved for villagers. It is a good place to rest tired legs.

blocks.title: The layered paddies of Hungduan Poblacion

children.text: Around the town center where the municipal hall stands, houses and paddies are stacked tightly on steep slopes. If Hapao is wide and soft, this side is high and dense. The smoke from cooking fires drifting over the paddies at dusk is memorable.

blocks.title: Watch the Punnuk and Huwah rituals

children.text: This tug-of-war ritual is held in the Hapao River after the harvest, around
August
. In 2026 Punnuk was held on
August 22
, and the Huwah celebration drew 2,267 attendees, the most ever recorded. Dates change every year, so check the latest announcements.

blocks.title: Stop at the Bokiawan boundary viewpoint

children.text: Bokiawan, on the boundary where the road passes from Banaue into Hungduan, looks down over a valley with the road and paddies stretching along it. It is too good to just glance at through a jeepney window, so it is worth getting out for a quick photo.

blocks.title: Hear about tinawon rice and farming

children.text: The people of Hungduan generally grow tinawon, a heirloom rice that comes in red and white varieties, once a year. If you ask your guide or host about transplanting, weeding and harvesting, you will see the terraces differently, and the rice you taste at the table will mean more.
Mount Napulawan, south of Hungduan, is the second-highest peak in Ifugao at around
. It is for travelers with mountain experience who climb with a guide; most visitors will find the paddy trekking more than enough.

9–11 hours
from Manila to Banaue, and a one-way fare is roughly

items.title: From Banaue to Hapao and Hungduan

children.text: Jeepneys to Hapao and Hungduan leave from the terminal in front of the Banaue market. The fare is about
to Hapao and about
to Hungduan Poblacion, and the ride takes about
1 hour
Jeepneys to Hungduan Poblacion run only three or four times a day between
noon and 5 p.m.
, while there are several to Hapao even in the morning. For the return, it is safest to travel from the morning until about
2 p.m.
If you miss a vehicle, you can charter a tricycle (about
for three people) or a jeepney (about
or more for ten people). Poblacion and Hapao are about
6–7km
apart, and a tricycle costs about
From Baguio, buses such as Ohayami and KMS take about
7–8 hours
to Banaue. From Bontoc, vans and jeepneys take about

for around
If you come from Sagada, travel through Bontoc the same way to reach Banaue, then continue into Hungduan.
From Manila to Hungduan it is about
400km
by road, passing through Lagawe and Banaue. The mountain road is narrow and winding, so driving in daytime is recommended.

If you have no car, it is easy to charter a vehicle with a driver from Banaue for a day and tour Hapao, Hungduan and Bokiawan in one go. Negotiate the price, and agree on whether waiting time is included.
Hapao and Poblacion are too far apart to walk between. Use a tricycle for short distances and walk through the paddies.
Public transport is scarce, so it is wise to ask your host first about chartered vehicles and shared-ride timetables.
The Hungduan paddies differ from village to village and year to year, but generally they are flooded and planted between
November and February
so that they reflect the sky, the rice grows and fills the valley with green from
March to May
, and the grain ripens to gold for harvest from
June to August
. The most recommended time is
April to May
, when the green is deepest.
The high elevation keeps the air cool, with temperatures of roughly
through the year and about 2,800mm of rain annually. The dry season from
December to June
is good for walking because the paths are dry and the sky is clear, but in the rainy season from
July to October
showers and fog are frequent, and typhoon landslides can cut the Banaue–Hungduan road. Punnuk and Huwah are held around
August
after the harvest, but the dates change every year, so check the latest announcements.

Lodging in Hungduan is concentrated in two places, along the road at Hapao and in Poblacion. Hapao has a few traveler guesthouses right beside the road, and Poblacion has simple lodges near the municipal hall. Prices run about ₱300–1,500 per night, with shared bathrooms the norm, and it is best not to expect hot water or Wi-Fi. Rooms can run short in peak season, so confirm in advance by phone or message from Banaue.

The food is simple mountain fare. Guesthouse restaurants sell eggs, fried rice, stir-fried vegetables, and chicken or pork dishes, and some serve tinawon, the heirloom rice grown locally. During rituals and village feasts, people share food and drink together and give thanks for the year's harvest. There are few shops, so bring snacks and water from Banaue.
There are no ATMs in Hungduan and cards are hard to use. Prepare cash in Banaue for the registration fee, guide, lodging and meals.
It is usual to write your name and purpose of visit at the registration office and be assigned a guide. Guide fees become village income, so pay the set rate according to the number of people.
Jeepneys to Hapao also run in the morning, but those to Hungduan Poblacion cluster after noon. Check the timetable in Banaue the day before.
Trekking shoes or shoes with good grip are essential. Paddy walls are very slippery when wet, so sneakers are safer than sandals.
At this altitude, dawn and night are chilly. Bring a thin windbreaker and a rain jacket.
Mobile signal barely reaches beyond the village center. Download offline maps.
To see rituals such as Punnuk and Huwah, book lodging and a guide much earlier and check local announcements.
Early morning and late afternoon give soft light and show the steps of the paddies clearly in photos.
Paddy walls are barely wide enough for one person, and many have a deep drop on one side. Stop completely when taking photos, and after rain follow your guide because the stones are slippery.
Do not step on or knock down paddy walls or walk into the paddies. A fallen stone wall has to be rebuilt by the villagers themselves.
When watching rituals and village events, do not stand in front and get in the way, and ask permission before photographing people. Follow instructions at ritual sites.
During typhoons and the rainy season, landslides can block the Banaue–Hungduan road. Leave a spare day in your schedule for the return.
Jeepney, entry rules and fares change often. Before you go, check the latest information with Hungduan's tourism office or your lodging.
Bogyah Hot Spring is reported to be reserved for villagers after about 4 p.m., so arrive early. Take your trash with you.
